automatic.answer: This is a small, dependency-free JavaScript ES-module project for validating balanced and correctly nested parentheses, square brackets, and braces. Its core is the synchronous `solve(s)` function in `src/core.mjs`, which uses a stack; `src/service.mjs` exposes a thin `execute(...args)` wrapper, and Node’s built-in test runner provides one smoke test. One important bug is that `solve` returns true without checking whether the stack is empty, so unmatched opening brackets incorrectly pass validation.

This is a small, dependency-free JavaScript ES-module service that validates balanced, correctly nested brackets: (), [], and {}. Its current context marker is INTERVIEW-111-feda68c18ab58993-PATCH-5cd51362749c.

The core is the synchronous `solve(s)` in `src/core.mjs`: it pushes opening brackets onto a stack, checks closing brackets against the latest opening, and requires an empty stack at the end; empty input is valid. `src/service.mjs` provides a thin `execute(...args)` wrapper, while `npm test` runs one smoke test through Node’s built-in test runner.

rows.source: function solve(n,edges){const degree=Array(n).fill(0),out=[];for(const[a,b]of edges)degree[b]++;const q=[];for(let i=0;i<n;i++)if(!degree[i])q.push(i);while(q.length){q.sort((a,b)=>a-b);const u=q.shift();out.push(u);for(const[a,b]of edges)if(a===u&&!--degree[b])q.push(b);}return out.length===n-1?out:[];}

Context marker: INTERVIEW-113-79388915d92f9818.

The bug is in `src/core.mjs`, specifically `return out.length===n-1?out:[];`: a complete topological ordering requires exactly `n` vertices, not `n-1`.

A smallest valid counterexample is `solve(1, [])`. The sole vertex has indegree zero, so the queue starts as `[0]`; processing it produces `out = [0]` and empties the queue. The final check evaluates `1 === 0` as false, returning `[]`; the required result is `[0]`.

rows.source: function solve(s,t){const need=new Set(t);let best="";for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<=s.length;j++){const w=s.slice(i,j);if([...need].every(c=>w.includes(c))&&(!best||w.length<best.length))best=w;}return best;}

This is a dependency-free JavaScript character-window service, marked INTERVIEW-118-28a0aab1502f6c2e. It should return the shortest substring of s containing every character of t with multiplicity, choosing the leftmost on ties and returning empty when impossible.

src/core.mjs exports synchronous solve(s,t) and searches all nonempty substrings; src/service.mjs exposes execute as a thin forwarding wrapper. The project uses ES modules, and npm test runs a Node built-in smoke test through that wrapper.

The current core incorrectly uses a Set and presence checks, so it ignores repeated-character requirements in t; the smoke test does not catch this.

A smallest valid counterexample is `solve([{key:1,id:"a"},{key:1,id:"b"}])`. At `i=1`, `j>0` and `1>=1` are true, so the records swap; `j` becomes zero and the loop exits. This is a dependency-free JavaScript priority-record service, marked INTERVIEW-119-3bbe708536d228f4. Its contract is to sort records by ascending numeric key, preserve input order for equal keys, and leave the input unchanged.

src/core.mjs exports synchronous solve(records), cloning the records and sorting them with insertion sort; src/service.mjs provides the thin execute wrapper. The project uses ES modules, and npm test runs a Node built-in smoke test through that wrapper. Currently, the core’s >= comparison swaps equal-key records, violating the stable-order requirement; the smoke test does not cover ties.

Current marker: INTERVIEW-120-bf2722f122d8d3ba.

The bug is in `src/core.mjs`: `if(p===".."&&st.length)st.pop();else st.push(p);`. When `..` occurs at root, the condition is false and `else st.push(p)` stores it instead of ignoring it, violating the requirement not to go above root.

A smallest valid counterexample is `solve("/..")`: the initial empty segment is skipped; then `..` encounters an empty stack and is pushed. Actual result: `"/.."`. Required result: `"/"`. No implementation changes yet.

rounds.answer:
The exact marker is INTERVIEW-82-4ea5f106bcaba44d. The task is to return whether all n courses can finish, with each [a,b] meaning b must precede a.

Approach: use Kahn’s topological sort. Build edges b → a and incoming-edge counts, queue all courses with count zero, then process them and decrement their dependents’ counts. Return true exactly when all n courses are processed.

Invariant: each remaining course’s count equals its incoming edges from unprocessed courses, so a zero-count course is safe to take. If processing stops early, every remaining course has an unmet prerequisite; following those dependencies must encounter a cycle.

Boundary cases: no courses or no prerequisites returns true; isolated courses and disconnected components must all be included; a self-loop or a cycle anywhere returns false. Duplicate pairs work if counted and decremented consistently. Course-label conventions and invalid-input behavior are not specified in the screenshot.

Time and space are O(n + p), where p is the number of prerequisite pairs. No implementation yet.

rounds.answer:
Marker: INTERVIEW-83-79d4678a8d054287.

Approach: copy every image row, record the starting pixel’s color, then use an iterative stack or queue to visit its same-color region through up, down, left, and right neighbors. Recolor pixels when adding them to the traversal so they cannot be added twice. Return the copy, leaving the original unchanged.

Invariant: every discovered pixel belongs to the starting pixel’s orthogonally connected original-color region; recolored pixels also serve as visited markers. Following every eligible neighbor eventually covers exactly that region.

Boundary cases: if newColor equals the starting color, return the independent copy immediately to avoid looping. Single-pixel images, edge and corner starts, and disconnected same-color regions work naturally; diagonal-only connections remain unchanged. Empty images and invalid coordinates have no specified behavior in the attachment.

For N pixels, copying and traversal take O(N) time and O(N) space.

Marker: INTERVIEW-84-e03f610d375ef664.

Approach: use breadth-first search from the top-left zero cell, exploring all eight neighboring directions. Track visited cells separately, marking them when enqueued, and start at distance 1 because path length counts cells. Return the distance when reaching the bottom-right; return -1 if the queue empties.

Invariant: BFS processes cells in nondecreasing distance, so each cell’s first discovery gives its shortest path length. Marking on enqueue prevents duplicate processing.

Boundary cases: either endpoint blocked means -1; a single zero cell returns 1, while a single one returns -1. Diagonal moves are allowed, even between blocked orthogonal neighbors. Unreachable destinations return -1; an empty grid, if permitted, also returns -1.

For an n × n grid, time and space are O(n²).

Marker: INTERVIEW-85-a6e8644ec1fe456e.

Approach: track top, bottom, left, and right boundaries. Append the top edge rightward and increment top; append the right edge downward and decrement right; if rows remain, append the bottom edge leftward and decrement bottom; if columns remain, append the left edge upward and increment left. Repeat while both boundary ranges are valid.

Invariant: before each iteration, the boundaries enclose exactly the unvisited rectangle, and the output contains every cell outside it exactly once in clockwise spiral order.

Boundary cases: [] or zero columns returns []; a single cell appears once. Single rows, single columns, and an odd-sized matrix’s center require the boundary checks to prevent duplicates. Rectangular matrices work without modification to the input. Time is O(rows × columns), with O(1) auxiliary space excluding the output.

Use four boundaries—top, bottom, left, and right—to track the unvisited rectangle. Traverse its top edge rightward, right edge downward, bottom edge leftward, and left edge upward, shrinking each boundary afterward. Check that boundaries still overlap before traversing the bottom and left edges, preventing duplicates for a remaining single row or column; this takes O(rows × columns) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding the output.

rounds.answer:
The exact current marker is INTERVIEW-86-78e9f9d31c8a078a. The project specifies a single JavaScript function, solve(matrix), that returns a new square matrix rotated 90 degrees clockwise, without modifying the input; no implementation is supplied.

Approach: allocate a separate n × n result and map each input cell [row][col] to result[col][n - 1 - row]. The invariant is that every processed input cell occupies its correct rotated position, while the input remains unchanged; this mapping fills each output position exactly once. Time and additional space are both O(n²).

Boundary cases: an empty matrix returns an empty matrix; a 1 × 1 matrix returns a new matrix containing the same value. Repeated values require no special handling, and non-square or malformed inputs are outside the stated contract.

Marker: INTERVIEW-87-48e34b4b8e7e60a5.

Approach: scan the grid; whenever an unvisited numeric 1 is found, use iterative DFS or BFS to count its island, exploring only up, down, left, and right. Mark cells visited when adding them to the worklist, and track the largest completed area without modifying the input.

Invariant: each land cell is counted at most once; each traversal counts exactly the land reachable from its starting cell, and the running maximum is the largest completed island.

Boundary cases: an empty grid or empty rows return 0; all zeros return 0; a single 1 returns 1; diagonal ones remain separate; an all-ones rectangular grid returns rows × columns. Bounds checks prevent traversal outside the grid.

Time: O(rows × columns). Auxiliary space: O(rows × columns) for visited cells and the worklist.

Marker: INTERVIEW-88-55ce5372eea6c80d.

Approach: use one pointer per sorted list. For each current pair, compute start = max of their starts and end = min of their ends; append [start, end] if start <= end. Advance the interval ending first, or both when their ends match; stop when either list is exhausted.

Invariant: all intersections involving previously discarded intervals have been reported exactly once. Advancing the earlier-ending interval is safe because subsequent intervals in the other list start beyond that endpoint.

Boundary cases: either list empty returns []; separated intervals produce no intersection; touching endpoints produce [x, x]. Also handle point intervals, containment, equal ends, and one interval intersecting several in the other list. Inputs need not be modified.

Time: O(a.length + b.length); auxiliary space: O(1), excluding the returned intersections.

automatic.answer:
The screen shows Interview 88: interval intersections, with marker INTERVIEW-88-55ce5372eea6c80d. The task is to define solve(a,b), returning intersections of two sorted lists of disjoint closed intervals; touching endpoints count as a point intersection.

Use two pointers: compute start = max of the current starts and end = min of the current ends, and append [start, end] whenever start <= end. Advance the interval ending first, or both if their ends match, because that interval cannot overlap any later interval in the other list. The invariant is that all intersections involving discarded intervals have already been recorded.

Empty inputs return []; nonoverlapping intervals produce nothing; [[1,2]] and [[2,3]] produce [[2,2]]. Time is O(a.length + b.length), with O(1) auxiliary space excluding the result. The required interface has no imports, exports, or stdin/stdout handling.

rounds.answer:
Marker: INTERVIEW-89-c2b0248566d03d13.

Approach: use a sweep line over meeting starts and ends, tracking the active count and its maximum. Process ends before starts at the same time because intervals are half-open; ignore zero-duration intervals [t,t), which occupy no time. The maximum active count is the minimum number of rooms needed.

Invariant: after processing all events at time t, the active count equals the number of meetings satisfying start ≤ t < end. The recorded maximum is the greatest simultaneous occupancy seen so far: that many rooms are necessary, and reusing released rooms makes them sufficient.

Boundary cases: empty input or only zero-duration meetings returns 0; touching meetings reuse one room; overlapping, nested, or duplicate nonempty meetings count separately. Sort events to handle unsorted input. Time is O(n log n), with O(n) auxiliary space; reversed intervals are not specified by the attachment.

Marker: INTERVIEW-90-a45d120fff367980.

Approach: ignore empty lists and use a min-heap containing one current value from each nonempty list, while tracking their maximum. Evaluate [minimum, maximum], keeping the narrowest range and, on equal widths, the smaller left endpoint. Advance the list supplying the minimum; stop when that list is exhausted.

Invariant: the heap contains one representative from every participating list, so each candidate covers them all. Advancing the minimum is sufficient: keeping it while advancing other lists cannot reduce the maximum or improve the range.

Boundary cases: duplicates and negative values work normally; a shared value gives width zero; one nonempty list returns its smallest value twice. Empty lists impose no requirement, but TASK.md does not specify the result when all lists are empty or lists itself is empty—what should that return?

For N total values across k nonempty lists, time is O(N log(k + 1)) and auxiliary space is O(k).

The exact current marker is INTERVIEW-91-f051c6d187cd7054. The screen asks for JavaScript solve(intervals,interval): insert a closed interval into sorted, disjoint intervals, merging overlaps and touching endpoints, and return the result without stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Approach: scan left to right in three phases. Copy intervals whose end is strictly less than the new start; then merge intervals whose start is at most the current merged end, updating both bounds; finally append the merged interval and all remaining intervals.

Invariant: the output prefix is sorted, disjoint, and finalized; during merging, the working interval is exactly the union of the new interval and everything absorbed so far. Once the next start exceeds the merged end, sorted order guarantees that no later interval can overlap it.

Boundary cases include empty input, insertion before or after everything, insertion into a gap, containment in either direction, spanning multiple intervals, and zero-length intervals. Equal endpoints must merge—for example, [1,2] and [2,3] become [1,3]. The scan takes O(n) time and O(n) output space, with O(1) auxiliary space excluding the result.

Marker: INTERVIEW-92-e1b132e4c1d2c350.

Approach: use a JavaScript Map ordered from least to most recently used. For a successful get, record the value and move its entry to the end; for a miss, record -1 without changing recency. For put, delete any existing entry and insert the new value at the end; if capacity is exceeded, evict the first entry.

Invariant: after each operation, the Map contains at most capacity entries, stores each key’s latest value, and its order exactly represents recency. The result array contains one value per get, in operation order.

Boundary cases: empty operations return []; capacity 1 evicts on insertion of a different key; replacement puts refresh recency without increasing size; repeated misses leave recency unchanged. A stored value of -1 must be distinguished from a miss using Map.has, not the value itself.

Expected time: O(number of operations). Space: O(capacity + number of gets), including the returned results.

Marker: INTERVIEW-93-77e973bed960d8cb.

Approach: process operations in order, using a Map from each key to its value and expiration time, putTime + ttl. A put replaces that key’s previous entry. A get returns null if the key is missing or now >= expiration; otherwise, it returns the stored value. Expired entries can be deleted lazily on access.

Invariant: each stored entry represents the latest put for its key, and a get returns its value only while now < expiration. Entries may remain stored after expiration, but must never be returned as valid.

Boundary cases: empty operations return []; missing keys return null; a get exactly at expiration returns null; zero TTL expires immediately; overwriting resets both value and expiration. Operations with equal timestamps still execute in their supplied order, and checking presence explicitly preserves valid falsy values such as 0 or false.

Expected time: O(m), assuming constant-time Map operations. Space: O(k + g), for distinct stored keys and returned get results. No implementation yet.

automatic.answer:
This project is a TTL cache simulation, marked INTERVIEW-93-77e973bed960d8cb—not the earlier LRU cache task. Its only supplied file, TASK.md, specifies JavaScript solve(operations), which processes timestamped put/get operations in nondecreasing time order and returns the get results.

The natural architecture is a single operation-processing loop backed by a map storing each key’s value and expiration time, putTime + ttl. A get returns null if the key is absent or now >= its expiration; otherwise, it returns the stored value. No implementation files are supplied, and the contract requires no stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Marker: INTERVIEW-94-fc99e4be4ba9a341.

Approach: scan the nondecreasing times, computing Math.floor(time / windowMs). Track the current window and its accepted count; reset that count when the window changes. Accept an event only if the count is below limit, incrementing only on acceptance.

Invariant: the count equals the number of accepted events in the current window, and every processed event has its corresponding boolean. Sorted times mean a completed window is never revisited.

Boundary cases: empty times returns []; repeated timestamps share a quota; events exactly at a window boundary start a fresh quota; skipped windows require only one reset; limit = 0 rejects everything. These are fixed, not sliding, windows, so events immediately across a boundary have separate quotas. The screenshot does not specify parameter ranges; this approach assumes windowMs > 0 and a nonnegative integer limit.

Time: O(n). Auxiliary space: O(1), excluding the O(n) returned booleans.

rounds.answer:
Marker: INTERVIEW-95-33d6a83015139fab.

Approach: scan the nondecreasing event times, tracking tokens and the previous time, initially capacity and zero. Before each event, refill with min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate). Accept if tokens >= 1 and subtract one; otherwise reject without spending tokens.

Invariant: immediately before each acceptance check, tokens equals the available balance after continuous refill, capped at capacity. After the check, it also reflects the token spent if accepted; rejected events still advance the previous time.

Boundary cases: empty times returns []; simultaneous events receive no refill between them; exactly one token permits acceptance; fractional tokens accumulate but cannot fund an event until reaching one; long gaps never refill above capacity. With rate zero, only the initial tokens are available; with capacity zero, every event is rejected. The attachment does not specify numeric input bounds.

Time: O(n). Auxiliary space: O(1), plus O(n) for the returned booleans. No implementation yet.

automatic.answer:
This project is a token-bucket rate limiter, marked INTERVIEW-95-33d6a83015139fab. Its only supplied file, TASK.md, defines JavaScript solve(times,capacity,rate), returning one acceptance boolean per event.

The architecture is a single chronological scan tracking available tokens and the previous event time. Start with capacity tokens at time zero; before each event, refill by elapsed time × rate, capped at capacity, then accept and spend one token only if at least one is available. This takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, plus O(n) for the result; no imports, exports, or stdin/stdout are required.

rounds.answer:
The exact current marker is INTERVIEW-96-c985cec66927ff0e. The attachment specifies a streaming-median task for JavaScript solve(nums); it contains no implementation.

Use a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Insert each number into the appropriate heap, rebalance, then append the current median to the returned array.

The invariant is that every lower-half value is at most every upper-half value, and the lower heap has either the same size as the upper heap or one extra element. For odd counts, the median is the lower heap’s maximum; for even counts, average both heap roots. Each insertion takes O(log n), with O(n) total storage.

Boundary cases include empty input returning [], one element returning itself, duplicates, negative numbers, and fractional medians for even counts. JavaScript Number arithmetic also requires care if integer inputs or their sums exceed the safe-integer range; the attachment gives no numeric bounds.

automatic.answer: This is a small JavaScript algorithm project for calculating the running median: after each integer is inserted, `solve(nums)` returns the median so far, averaging the two middle values for even counts. The attachment contains only the task specification, so there’s no implemented architecture to review. A suitable design uses a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, keeping them balanced for O(log n) insertions and O(1) median lookups, with no imports, exports, or console I/O.

For solve(operations), process operations in order and maintain a Map from each key to its timestamp–value history. Set times are unique and increasing per key, so each set appends; each get binary-searches for the rightmost timestamp at or before its query time.

The invariant is that each history contains exactly the sets processed for that key, in strictly increasing timestamp order. During binary search, entries before the search boundary qualify and entries after it are too late; the last qualifying entry supplies the answer.

Boundary cases include empty operations, an unknown key, a query before the first timestamp, an exact timestamp match, a query between timestamps, and a query after the latest timestamp. Different keys remain independent, and query times need not increase. Sets take amortized O(1), gets O(log m) for a history of size m, and storage is O(s) for s sets, excluding results.

The toolbar obscures part of the specification, so I cannot confirm the required no-match return value or exact result format from this attachment. Those details need to be visible before implementation.

Marker: INTERVIEW-98-4571d36ea054ec2b.

Use one pass through events, maintaining a Set of seen IDs, a running total, and acceptedIds. For a new ID, record it, add its delta, and append the ID; ignore all later occurrences, even if their deltas differ.

Invariant: after every processed prefix, the Set and acceptedIds contain exactly its distinct IDs, acceptedIds preserves first-seen order, and total sums only those IDs’ first-occurrence deltas.

Marker: INTERVIEW-99-6db451fefcd29335.

Use a circular buffer with a head index and current size. For push, reject with false if full; otherwise store at (head + size) modulo capacity, increment size, and return true. For pop, return null if empty; otherwise remove the head value, advance head modulo capacity, decrement size, and return the value. Collect one result per operation.

Invariant: size stays between zero and capacity, and the size entries starting at head represent the accepted, unpopped values in FIFO order. Rejected pushes never change the queue.

Boundary cases: capacity zero rejects every push and returns null for every pop; check these conditions before any modulo operation. Empty operations return []; full queues do not overwrite; wraparound preserves order; duplicate values remain separate entries.

Each operation takes O(1) time. Queue storage is O(capacity), plus O(operations.length) for results.

This project is “bounded-fifo-queue,” marked INTERVIEW-99-6db451fefcd29335. It asks for JavaScript solve(capacity, operations), returning one result per operation: push returns whether it was accepted, and pop returns the oldest value or null when empty; full queues reject pushes without overwriting.

The attachment contains only TASK.md, so there is no existing implementation to review. A suitable architecture is a circular buffer with a head index and current size, giving O(1) work per operation and O(capacity) queue storage; capacity zero rejects every push.

Marker: INTERVIEW-100-aaa5e7cbb5a33ac1.

Approach: Use batched Kahn’s topological sort. For each edge [before, after], store after in before’s adjacency list and increment after’s indegree. Start with all zero-indegree tasks, sort the batch ascending, and process the entire batch while collecting newly unlocked tasks separately for the next batch.

Invariant: Each remaining task’s indegree counts prerequisites not yet completed, and every task in the current batch has all prerequisites in earlier batches. Keeping the next batch separate prevents a task from running alongside its prerequisite. If processing stops before all n tasks are completed, return null because a cycle remains.

Boundary cases: n = 0 returns []; no edges returns one ascending batch containing all task IDs; a chain gives singleton batches; disconnected tasks are included; self-loops and cycles return null, even when other components finish. Repeated edges work if each occurrence is counted and decremented consistently.

Time: O(n + edges.length + n log n) worst case, including sorting; space: O(n + edges.length).

automatic.answer:
The screen shows Interview 100, a dependency-batching task, marked INTERVIEW-100-aaa5e7cbb5a33ac1. Define solve(n, edges) to return parallel-ready batches of task IDs, sorted ascending within each batch, or null if dependencies contain a cycle.

Use an adjacency list and incoming-edge counts: collect all zero-count tasks as the current batch, then process that entire batch to unlock the next one. Keep newly unlocked tasks separate so they cannot run in the same batch as their prerequisites. If fewer than n tasks are processed, return null; n = 0 returns [], and tasks without dependencies belong in the first batch.

Time is O(n + edges.length + n log n), including batch sorting; space is O(n + edges.length).
